justice: The street allocates most of its width to multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while no clearly visible sidewalk zone is provided in the main field of view, indicating uneven distribution of space among road users.
There is no visible dedicated bicycle lane, cycle track, or bicycle parking, so cyclists appear to receive less infrastructure support than drivers.
Accessibility is limited because no curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free pedestrian connections are visible along either edge of the roadway.
safety: The roadway is very wide and straight, a geometry that can encourage higher vehicle speeds and increase risk for all road users.
Lane markings are clear and the pavement surface appears smooth and well maintained, which supports predictable vehicle movement.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, improving baseline visibility, but there are no visible crosswalks, refuge islands, or traffic-calming devices to protect pedestrians and cyclists.
livability: Dense tree lines and landscaped planting strips on both sides add environmental quality, but the corridor lacks visible shops, seating, or active frontages that support everyday street life.
The scene appears sparsely populated with no visible pedestrians, cyclists, or social activity, suggesting limited street vitality.
This reads more like an access road or low-activity corridor than a mixed-use public street, reducing its usefulness for daily social and civic life.
sustainability: Continuous rows of mature trees and planted verges provide meaningful green coverage and ecological value along the corridor.
The street design is dominated by car travel, with no visible bus stop, bike lane, or other strong support for low-carbon multimodal transport.
Large paved carriageway areas increase impervious surface coverage, and no visible permeable paving, bioswales, or stormwater facilities can be identified.
aesthetics: The long perspective view, orderly streetlight alignment, and consistent roadway edges create a visually coherent streetscape.
Dense greenery on the right side and landscaped planting on the left improve visual softness and overall scenic quality.
The visible power transmission tower and overhead utility lines introduce industrial visual elements that slightly reduce the otherwise clean landscape appearance.
comfort: Tree cover along both sides can improve thermal comfort near the edges of the corridor, especially for people off the carriageway.
The road surface appears smooth and even, which benefits physical comfort for drivers and potentially cyclists, but there are no visible benches or pedestrian amenities.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the open, uncrowded setting feels calm, yet the wide vehicle-oriented roadway and absence of protected pedestrian space may feel uncomfortable for non-motorized users.
walkability: No clearly defined sidewalk is visible beside the travel lanes, which strongly reduces walkability for pedestrians.
There are no marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, curb extensions, or median refuges visible to support safe crossing of this wide road.
Although the corridor is visually open and lined with greenery, the street is fundamentally designed around motor traffic rather than continuous pedestrian movement.
bikeability: There is no visible protected bike lane, painted bike lane, or shoulder designated for cyclists, making bicycle use less supported.
The wide, straight carriageway may allow riding space, but it also likely encourages faster motor traffic, increasing perceived danger for cyclists.
No bicycle-specific markings, intersection treatments, or parking facilities are visible, so cycling convenience and network legibility appear low.
